claim: LXRs are transcriptional regulators of lipid homeostasis that have potent anti-inflammatory effects.
source: The liver X receptors (LXRs) are transcriptional regulators of lipid homeostasis that also have potent anti-inflammatory effects.
evidence: This is a general statement about LXR function that is supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The molecular basis for LXR's anti-inflammatory effects has been proposed to involve the indirect tethering of LXRs to inflammatory gene promoters.
source: The molecular basis for their anti-inflammatory effects is incompletely understood, but has been proposed to involve the indirect tethering of LXRs to inflammatory gene promoters.
evidence: This refers to prior hypotheses in the literature about LXR mechanism.

claim: The ability of LXRs to repress inflammatory gene expression in cells and mice derives primarily from their ability to regulate lipid metabolism through transcriptional activation.
source: Here we demonstrate that the ability of LXRs to repress inflammatory gene expression in cells and mice derives primarily from their ability to regulate lipid metabolism through transcriptional activation and can occur in the absence of SUMOylation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by multiple experiments shown in the figures.

claim: LXR-mediated inflammatory repression can occur in the absence of SUMOylation.
source: Here we demonstrate that the ability of LXRs to repress inflammatory gene expression in cells and mice derives primarily from their ability to regulate lipid metabolism through transcriptional activation and can occur in the absence of SUMOylation.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with SUMOylation site mutants shown in Figure 2.

claim: Abca1 is a critical mediator of LXR's anti-inflammatory effects.
source: Moreover, we identify the putative lipid transporter Abca1 as a critical mediator of LXR's anti-inflammatory effects.
evidence: This is supported by siRNA knockdown and genetic deletion experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Activation of LXR inhibits signaling from TLRs 2, 4 and 9 to their downstream NF-κB and MAPK effectors through Abca1-dependent changes in membrane lipid organization.
source: Activation of LXR inhibits signaling from TLRs 2, 4 and 9 to their downstream NF-κB and MAPK effectors through Abca1-dependent changes in membrane lipid organization that disrupt the recruitment of MyD88 and TRAF6.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 6, 7, 9, 10, and 11 showing effects on signaling pathways and membrane composition.

claim: Abca1-dependent changes in membrane lipid organization disrupt the recruitment of MyD88 and TRAF6.
source: Activation of LXR inhibits signaling from TLRs 2, 4 and 9 to their downstream NF-κB and MAPK effectors through Abca1-dependent changes in membrane lipid organization that disrupt the recruitment of MyD88 and TRAF6.
evidence: This is supported by membrane fractionation experiments shown in Figure 11.

claim: A common mechanism—direct transcriptional activation—underlies the dual biological functions of LXRs in metabolism and inflammation.
source: These data suggest that a common mechanism-direct transcriptional activation-underlies the dual biological functions of LXRs in metabolism and inflammation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: LXRs control the expression of genes involved in cholesterol, fatty acid and phospholipid metabolism through direct binding to LXR response elements (LXREs) in their target promoters.
source: LXRs control the expression of a battery of genes involved in cholesterol, fatty acid and phospholipid metabolism through direct binding to LXR response elements (LXREs) in their target promoters (Calkin and Tontonoz, 2012; Hong and Tontonoz, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: LXRs have the ability to antagonize inflammatory gene expression triggered by Toll-like receptor (TLR) activation.
source: In addition to their ability to activate the expression of genes linked to lipid metabolism, LXRs also have the ability to antagonize inflammatory gene expression triggered by Toll-like receptor (TLR) activation (Joseph et al., 2003, 2004; Castrillo et al., 2003a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: LXRs have been proposed to act on inflammatory promoters through mechanisms that do not involve DNA-binding domain recognition of LXREs.
source: Rather, they have been proposed to act on inflammatory promoters through mechanisms that do not involve DNA-binding domain recognition of LXREs.
evidence: This refers to prior hypotheses about LXR mechanism.

claim: The transrepression model postulates that LXRs become SUMOylated in response to LXR agonist and that this SUMOylated LXR monomer stabilizes repressive nuclear complexes on the promoters of inflammatory genes.
source: One proposed mechanism, termed 'transrepression', postulates that LXRs become SUMOylated in response to LXR agonist and that this SUMOylated LXR monomer stabilizes repressive nuclear complexes on the promoters of inflammatory genes.
evidence: This describes a prior model from the literature.

claim: Key features of the transrepression model include the requirement for receptor SUMOylation, the involvement of an LXR monomer, and the mechanistic separation of the transcriptional activation and repression functions of LXRs.
source: Key features of this model include the requirement for receptor SUMOylation, the involvement of an LXR monomer, and the mechanistic separation of the transcriptional activation and repression functions of LXRs (Ghisletti et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2009; Venteclef et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes features of a prior model supported by citations.

claim: The requirement for receptor SUMOylation in the repressive actions of LXRs on inflammatory genes in cells and animals remains to be tested.
source: Although several lines of evidence have supported the transrepression model, the requirement for receptor SUMOylation in the repressive actions of LXRs on inflammatory genes in cells and animals remains to be tested.
evidence: This is a statement about gaps in prior knowledge.

claim: The ability of LXRs to antagonize endogenous inflammatory gene expression in cultured cells and in vivo is a consequence of changes in cellular lipid metabolism.
source: We demonstrate here that the ability of LXRs to antagonize endogenous inflammatory gene expression in cultured cells and in vivo is a consequence of changes in cellular lipid metabolism.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The ability of LXRs to activate transcription of the Abca1 sterol transporter and thereby alter membrane cholesterol homeostasis has a secondary effect on inflammatory signaling through inhibition of NF-κB and MAPK signaling pathways downstream of TLRs.
source: We show that the ability of LXRs to activate transcription of the Abca1 sterol transporter, and thereby alter membrane cholesterol homeostasis, has a secondary effect on inflammatory signaling through inhibition of NF-κB and MAPK signaling pathways downstream of TLRs.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 3, 6, 7, and 9.

claim: Direct transcriptional activation underlies the dual biological functions of LXRs in metabolism and inflammation.
source: These data present a unified view of LXR-dependent gene regulation in which direct transcriptional activation underlies the dual biological functions of LXRs in metabolism and inflammation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the experimental data.

claim: Local membrane composition is important in the activation of TLR signaling pathways.
source: They further emphasize the importance of local membrane composition in the activation of TLR signaling pathways.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing effects of membrane cholesterol on TLR signaling.

claim: siRNA-mediated knockdown of RXRα and RXRβ in primary mouse macrophages blunted the ability of LXR agonist to repress LPS-induced expression of endogenous inflammatory genes.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that siRNA-mediated knockdown of RXRα and RXRβ in primary mouse macrophages blunted the ability of LXR agonist to repress the LPS-induced expression of the endogenous inflammatory genes Nos2, Il1β, Ccl2, Cxcl1, Tnfα, Cox2 and Il6 (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and supplementary figures.

claim: LXR acts to repress inflammation as a heterodimer with RXR.
source: This observation suggested that LXR was acting to repress inflammation as a heterodimer with RXR in our system.
evidence: This is inferred from the RXR knockdown experiments.

claim: GW3965 did not induce the canonical LXR target gene Abca1 in LXR-deficient MEFs or macrophages.
source: The synthetic LXR agonist GW3965 did not induce the canonical LXR target gene Abca1, nor did it repress LPS-induced inflammatory gene expression, in LXR-deficient MEFs or macrophages (Figures 1B,C, 2A,B) (Castrillo et al., 2003a, 2003b; Joseph et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 1B, 1C, 2A, and 2B.

claim: GW3965 did not repress LPS-induced inflammatory gene expression in LXR-deficient MEFs or macrophages.
source: The synthetic LXR agonist GW3965 did not induce the canonical LXR target gene Abca1, nor did it repress LPS-induced inflammatory gene expression, in LXR-deficient MEFs or macrophages (Figures 1B,C, 2A,B) (Castrillo et al., 2003a, 2003b; Joseph et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 1B, 1C, 2A, and 2B.

claim: When LXR-deficient cells were reconstituted with wild-type LXRα, GW3965 treatment simultaneously induced Abca1 expression and repressed LPS-induced inflammatory gene expression.
source: However, when LXR-deficient cells were reconstituted with wild-type LXRα, GW3965 treatment simultaneously induced Abca1 expression and repressed LPS-induced inflammatory gene expression (Ccl2 and Cxcl1) (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: Both the activating and repressive effects of GW3965 are entirely mediated by LXRs.
source: These results establish that both the activating and repressive effects of GW3965 under our experimental conditions are entirely mediated by LXRs.
evidence: This is concluded from the reconstitution experiments.

claim: Many synthetic LXR agonists, including GW3965 and T0901317, can exhibit LXR-independent effects on gene expression, especially when used at concentrations higher than employed in this study.
source: This is important to emphasize because many synthetic LXR agonists, including GW3965 and T0901317, can exhibit LXR-independent effects on gene expression, especially when used at concentrations higher than employed here.
evidence: This is a statement based on knowledge of LXR agonist properties.

claim: The level of reconstituted LXR protein expression in the cells was within the physiologic range and restored target gene expression to physiologic levels.
source: It is also important to note that this approach does not involve supraphysiologic overexpression of LXRs, as the level of reconstituted protein expression in these cells was within the physiologic range and restored target gene expression to physiologic levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Agonist treatment induced Abca1 and repressed the levels of Ccl2 and Cxcl1 in AF1-deletion mutant cells.
source: Agonist treatment induced Abca1 and repressed the levels of Ccl2 and Cxcl1 in AF1-deletion mutant cells.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: Both the activation and repression activities of LXR were completely abolished in DNA binding domain- (DBD), ligand binding domain- (LBD) or AF2-deletion mutant cells.
source: However, both the activation and repression activities of LXR were completely abolished in DNA binding domain- (DBD), ligand binding domain- (LBD) or AF2-deletion mutant cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: The DBD, LBD and AF2 domains, but not the AF1 domain, are critical for both transactivation and repression by LXR.
source: Thus, the DBD, LBD and AF2 domains, but not the AF1 domain, are critical for both transactivation and repression by LXR.
evidence: This is concluded from the domain deletion experiments.

claim: An LXR mutant defective in its ability to recruit co-activators, L439A/E441A, was unable to induce Abca1 or to repress inflammatory genes in both MEFs and iBMDM.
source: Furthermore, an LXR mutant defective in its ability to recruit co-activators, L439A/E441A (Tzukerman et al., 1994; Bastie et al., 2000), was unable to induce Abca1 or to repress inflammatory genes in both MEFs and iBMDM (Figure 1C, Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), strongly suggesting that gene activation and inflammatory repression are mechanistically linked.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 1C, 2B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, along with citations.

claim: Gene activation and inflammatory repression by LXR are mechanistically linked.
source: Furthermore, an LXR mutant defective in its ability to recruit co-activators, L439A/E441A (Tzukerman et al., 1994; Bastie et al., 2000), was unable to induce Abca1 or to repress inflammatory genes in both MEFs and iBMDM (Figure 1C, Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), strongly suggesting that gene activation and inflammatory repression are mechanistically linked.
evidence: This is inferred from the L439A/E441A mutant experiments.

claim: Mutants of LXRα and LXRβ that lack the SUMOylation sites previously identified were capable of inducing Abca1 and repressing inflammatory genes in both MEFs and iBMDM.
source: In contrast to activation-defective LXR proteins, mutants of LXRα and LXRβ that lack the SUMOylation sites previously identified (Ghisletti et al., 2007) were capable of inducing Abca1 and repressing inflammatory genes in both MEFs and iBMDM (Figure 2A,B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 2A, 2B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mutation of three additional residues in the hinge region of the receptor predicted to be likely SUMOylation sites had no effect on LXR-dependent repression of Cxcl1 or Ccl2.
source: We considered the possibility that alternative SUMOylation sites might be employed, however, mutation of three additional residues in the hinge region of the receptor predicted to be likely SUMOylation sites also had no effect on LXR-dependent repression of Cxcl1 or Ccl2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: LXR SUMOylation site mutants were capable of mediating ligand-dependent repression of a broad array of inflammatory genes.
source: However, transcriptional profiling revealed that LXR SUMOylation site mutants were capable of mediating ligand-dependent repression of a broad array of inflammatory genes (e.g., those annotated with the 'Immune system process' GO term; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Knocking down Ubc9 or Hdac4 by siRNA in iBMDM did not block inflammatory repression by LXR.
source: We further tested whether the SUMOylation machinery reported to target LXR was required for inflammatory repression in our system. Knocking down Ubc9 or Hdac4 by siRNA in iBMDM did not block repression (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: SUMOylation-dependent transrepression could not account for the inhibitory actions of LXR on inflammatory gene expression in this system.
source: Thus, SUMOylation-dependent transrepression could not account for the inhibitory actions of LXR on inflammatory gene expression in our system.
evidence: This is concluded from the SUMOylation mutant and knockdown experiments.

claim: Knockdown of Abca1 substantially impaired the ability of LXR agonists to repress inflammatory gene expression.
source: Surprisingly, we found that knockdown of Abca1, a gene critical for cellular cholesterol efflux (Oram, 2003), substantially impaired the ability of LXR agonists to repress inflammatory gene expression (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by siRNA knockdown data in Figure 3A.

claim: Knockdown of Abcg1 or Apoe had no effect on inflammatory repression by LXR.
source: By contrast, knockdown of Abcg1 or Apoe, two other LXR target genes involved in metabolism, had no effect on inflammatory repression (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by siRNA knockdown data in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ability of LXR agonist to repress inflammation was markedly inhibited in macrophages from myeloid-specific Abca1−/− mice.
source: We corroborated these results by analyzing the effects of LXR agonist in BMDM from myeloid-specific Abca1−/− mice. Again, the ability of LXR agonist to repress inflammation was markedly inhibited in the genetic absence of Abca1 (Figure 3B), but not Abcg1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data from Abca1-deficient mice in Figure 3B.

claim: Most of the genes annotated with the 'Immune system process' GO term were not repressed by LXR activation in Abca1-deficient macrophages.
source: This analysis revealed that most of the genes annotated with the 'Immune system process' GO term were not repressed by LXR activation in Abca1-deficient macrophages (Figure 3C), suggesting that LXR-induced Abca1 expression is broadly important for LXR-mediated repression.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data in Figure 3C.

claim: LXR-induced Abca1 expression is broadly important for LXR-mediated repression.
source: This analysis revealed that most of the genes annotated with the 'Immune system process' GO term were not repressed by LXR activation in Abca1-deficient macrophages (Figure 3C), suggesting that LXR-induced Abca1 expression is broadly important for LXR-mediated repression.
evidence: This is inferred from the microarray data.

claim: The ability of dexamethasone to repress inflammatory gene expression was preserved in Abca1−/− cells.
source: The ability of dexamethasone to repress inflammatory gene expression was preserved in Abca1−/− cells, indicating that distinct mechanisms are involved in transcriptional repression by LXR and GR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Distinct mechanisms are involved in transcriptional repression by LXR and GR.
source: The ability of dexamethasone to repress inflammatory gene expression was preserved in Abca1−/− cells, indicating that distinct mechanisms are involved in transcriptional repression by LXR and GR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from the dexamethasone experiments in Abca1-deficient cells.

claim: LXR-dependent induction of Abca1 contributes to the maintenance of sterol homeostasis by promoting the efflux of cellular cholesterol to extracellular acceptors such as ApoA-I and ApoE.
source: Prior work has shown that LXR-dependent induction of Abca1 contributes to the maintenance of sterol homeostasis by promoting the efflux of cellular cholesterol to extracellular acceptors such as ApoA-I and ApoE (Santamarina-Fojo et al., 2001; Oram, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Tangier disease is a severe HDL deficiency syndrome that is caused by mutations in the ABCA1 gene.
source: Tangier disease is a severe HDL deficiency syndrome that is caused by mutations in the ABCA1 gene.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge.

claim: LXR target genes were induced at similar levels in normal and Tangier fibroblasts in response to activation by synthetic agonist.
source: LXR target genes were induced at similar levels in normal (healthy donor) and Tangier fibroblasts in response to activation by synthetic agonist (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4A.

claim: LXR activation with ligand repressed inflammatory gene expression in normal cells, but this response was abrogated in Tangier fibroblasts.
source: While LXR activation with ligand repressed inflammatory gene expression in normal cells, this response was abrogated in Tangier fibroblasts (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: When Abca1-deficient cells were reconstituted with wild-type Abca1, inflammatory gene expression was repressed by LXR activation.
source: When Abca1-deficient cells were reconstituted with wild-type Abca1, inflammatory gene expression was repressed by LXR activation; however, this effect was lost in cells expressing the N935S or C1477R mutants (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: The repressive effect of LXR activation on inflammatory gene expression was lost in cells expressing the Abca1 N935S or C1477R mutants.
source: When Abca1-deficient cells were reconstituted with wild-type Abca1, inflammatory gene expression was repressed by LXR activation; however, this effect was lost in cells expressing the N935S or C1477R mutants (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: Cholesterol transport by Abca1 is critical for inflammatory repression in human cells.
source: These data suggest that cholesterol transport by Abca1 is critical for inflammatory repression in human cells and that effective LXR-dependent inhibition of inflammation requires the ATP-dependent transporter function of Abca1.
evidence: This is inferred from the Abca1 mutant experiments.

claim: Effective LXR-dependent inhibition of inflammation requires the ATP-dependent transporter function of Abca1.
source: These data suggest that cholesterol transport by Abca1 is critical for inflammatory repression in human cells and that effective LXR-dependent inhibition of inflammation requires the ATP-dependent transporter function of Abca1.
evidence: This is inferred from the Abca1 mutant experiments.

claim: Cholesterol addition activated LXR target genes and repressed SREBP target genes.
source: As expected, cholesterol addition activated LXR target genes and repressed SREBP target genes, whereas cholesterol removal inhibited LXR target genes and induced SREBP target genes (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: Cholesterol removal inhibited LXR target genes and induced SREBP target genes.
source: As expected, cholesterol addition activated LXR target genes and repressed SREBP target genes, whereas cholesterol removal inhibited LXR target genes and induced SREBP target genes (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: Increasing the cholesterol content of the cell enhanced the induction of inflammatory genes by LPS.
source: Remarkably, increasing the cholesterol content of the cell also enhanced the induction of inflammatory genes by LPS.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: Decreasing cholesterol content inhibited the induction of inflammatory genes by LPS.
source: On the other hand, decreasing cholesterol content inhibited the induction of inflammatory genes (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: Regulation of membrane cholesterol content by LXRs may modulate inflammatory responses.
source: These data are consistent with the hypothesis that regulation of membrane cholesterol content by LXRs may modulate inflammatory responses.
evidence: This is inferred from the cholesterol manipulation experiments.

claim: Treatment of macrophages with LXR agonist inhibited the activation of ERK, p38 and JNK MAP kinases downstream of TLR4 activation.
source: We found that treatment of macrophages with LXR agonist inhibited the activation of ERK, p38 and JNK MAP kinases downstream of TLR4 activation (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: Reduced levels of phospho-ERK, phospho-p38 and phospho-JNK were observed in the setting of LXR activation.
source: Reduced levels of phospho-ERK, phospho-p38 and phospho-JNK were observed in the setting of LXR activation.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 6.

claim: The inhibitory effect of LXR agonist on MAPK signaling was mediated by LXRs, as it was not observed in LXR-deficient macrophages.
source: Importantly, this effect was mediated by LXRs, as it was not observed in LXR-deficient macrophages.
evidence: This is supported by data comparing wild-type and LXR-deficient cells in Figure 6.

claim: The ability of LXR agonist to inhibit ERK, p38 and JNK activation was severely impaired in cells lacking Abca1.
source: Remarkably, the ability of LXR agonist to inhibit ERK, p38 and JNK activation was severely impaired in cells lacking Abca1 (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: LXR agonist suppressed the activation of NF-κB signaling downstream of TLR4.
source: We also found that LXR agonist suppressed the activation of NF-κB signaling downstream of TLR4.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: Treatment of macrophages with GW3965 reduced the ratio of phospho-IκBα to total IκBα and reduced the nuclear abundance of p65.
source: Immunoblot analysis of whole cell lysates and nuclear extracts revealed that treatment of macrophages with GW3965 reduced the ratio of phospho-IκBα to total IκBα and reduced the nuclear abundance of p65 (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: The effects of LXR agonist on NF-κB signaling were LXR-dependent, as they were not observed in LXR-deficient macrophages.
source: These effects of agonist were also LXR-dependent, as they were not observed in LXR-deficient macrophages.
evidence: This is supported by data comparing wild-type and LXR-deficient cells in Figure 7.

claim: The ability of LXR agonist to suppress NF-κB signaling was abolished in Abca1-deficient macrophages.
source: Furthermore, the ability of LXR agonist to suppress NF-κB signaling was abolished in Abca1-deficient macrophages (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 7C and 7D.

claim: GW3965 inhibited p65 nuclear translocation in an LXR-dependent and Abca1-dependent manner.
source: Analysis of p65 localization by confocal immunofluorescence microscopy confirmed the ability of GW3965 to inhibit p65 nuclear translocation in an LXR-dependent and Abca1-dependent manner (Figure 7E,F).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figures 7E and 7F.

claim: The binding of p65 to the Nos2, IL1b and Ccl2 gene promoters was increased by LPS treatment.
source: The binding of p65 to the Nos2, IL1b and Ccl2 gene promoters was increased by LPS treatment as expected, whereas no binding was observed on the hemoglobin beta (Hbb2) gene promoter, which does not contain a p65 binding site (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data in Figure 8.

claim: No p65 binding was observed on the hemoglobin beta (Hbb2) gene promoter, which does not contain a p65 binding site.
source: The binding of p65 to the Nos2, IL1b and Ccl2 gene promoters was increased by LPS treatment as expected, whereas no binding was observed on the hemoglobin beta (Hbb2) gene promoter, which does not contain a p65 binding site (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data in Figure 8.

claim: LXR activation suppressed LPS-induced p65 recruitment to the Nos2s, Ccl2 and Il1b gene promoters.
source: We found that LXR activation suppressed LPS-induced p65 recruitment to the Nos2s, Ccl2 and Il1b gene promoters.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data in Figure 8.

claim: The inhibitory effect of LXR agonist on p65 recruitment was lost in Abca1-deficient macrophages.
source: Moreover, the inhibitory effect of LXR agonist on p65 recruitment was lost in Abca1-deficient macrophages (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data in Figure 8.

claim: LXR activation inhibits signaling through TLR4, and Abca1 expression is critical for this phenomenon.
source: Together, the data of Figures 6–8 demonstrate that LXR activation inhibits signaling through TLR4, and that Abca1 expression is critical for this phenomenon.
evidence: This is concluded from the data in Figures 6-8.

claim: LXR activation reduced the cholesterol content of Flotillin-enriched detergent-resistant membrane microdomains in wild-type but not LXR-deficient macrophages.
source: We found that LXR activation reduced the cholesterol content of Flotillin-enriched detergent-resistant membrane microdomains in wild-type type (<47% reduction) but not LXR-deficient macrophages (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by membrane fractionation data in Figure 9A.

claim: The reduction in cholesterol content of detergent-resistant membrane microdomains by LXR activation was not observed in Abca1-deficient macrophages.
source: Furthermore, this reduction in cholesterol content of detergent-resistant membrane microdomains was not observed in Abca1-deficient macrophages (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by membrane fractionation data in Figure 9B.

claim: The expression of ganglioside GM1, a marker of lipid rafts, was not altered by LXR agonist.
source: On the other hand, the expression of ganglioside GM1, a marker of lipid rafts, was not altered by LXR agonist (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 9C.

claim: LXR-dependent ABCA1 expression reduces the cholesterol content of detergent-resistant membrane microdomains without affecting the abundance of lipid rafts in the plasma membrane.
source: These results suggest that LXR-dependent ABCA1 expression reduces the cholesterol content of detergent-resistant membrane microdomains without affecting the abundance of lipid rafts in the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the membrane fractionation and flow cytometry data.

claim: Changes in membrane lipid content can affect inflammatory responses.
source: Accumulating evidence suggests that changes in membrane lipid content can affect inflammatory responses (Westerterp et al., 2013; Rong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: LXR-dependent Abca1 induction reduces raft cholesterol content and alters membrane fluidity.
source: Our membrane dynamics and biochemical studies indicate that LXR-dependent Abca1 induction reduces raft cholesterol content and alters membrane fluidity, suggesting a biophysical basis for the ability of LXR to inhibit TLR signaling.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 9.

claim: Plasma membrane rigidity was decreased in response to LXR activation.
source: As shown in Figure 9D, plasma membrane rigidity was decreased in response to LXR activation, consistent with the altered cholesterol distribution.
evidence: This is supported by laurdan fluorescence data in Figure 9D.

claim: The ability of LXR agonist treatment to affect plasma membrane fluidity in primary macrophages was largely dependent on Abca1 expression.
source: Furthermore, the ability of LXR agonist treatment to affect plasma membrane fluidity in primary macrophages was largely dependent on Abca1expression, as we did not observe a shift in laurdan signal in Abca1−/− macrophages (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is supported by laurdan fluorescence data in Figure 9D.

claim: LXR activation blunted the response to TLR2 and TLR9 agonists.
source: LXR activation blunted the response to TLR2 and TLR9 (Figure 10A,B), but did not affect the induction of viral response genes by TLR3 (Figure 10C).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 10A and 10B.

claim: LXR activation did not affect the induction of viral response genes by TLR3.
source: LXR activation blunted the response to TLR2 and TLR9 (Figure 10A,B), but did not affect the induction of viral response genes by TLR3 (Figure 10C).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 10C.

claim: Loss of Abca1 expression in macrophages inhibited the ability of LXR agonist to repress gene expression stimulated by TLR2 and TLR9 as well as by TLR4.
source: Furthermore, loss of Abca1 expression in macrophages inhibited the ability of LXR agonist to repress gene expression stimulated by TLR2 and TLR9 as well as by TLR4.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 10.

claim: LXR-dependent membrane lipid remodeling was targeting a component of the inflammatory signaling cascade common to TLRs 2, 4 and 9.
source: These observations suggested that LXR-dependent membrane lipid remodeling was targeting a component of the inflammatory signaling cascade common to TLRs 2, 4 and 9.
evidence: This is inferred from the TLR agonist experiments.

claim: The adaptor molecule MyD88 is commonly engaged by TLRs 2, 4 and 9 and links these receptors to the downstream activation of MAPKs and NF-κB.
source: The adaptor molecule MyD88 is commonly engaged by TLRs 2, 4 and 9 and links these receptors to the downstream activation of MAPKs and NF-κB, and ultimately to the induction of cytokine gene expression.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TLR signaling pathways.

claim: MyD88 links TLRs 2, 4 and 9 to the downstream activation of MAPKs and NF-κB, and ultimately to the induction of cytokine gene expression.
source: The adaptor molecule MyD88 is commonly engaged by TLRs 2, 4 and 9 and links these receptors to the downstream activation of MAPKs and NF-κB, and ultimately to the induction of cytokine gene expression.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TLR signaling pathways.

claim: TLR4 expression in plasma membrane was not affected by LXR activation.
source: Flow cytometry revealed that TLR4 expression in plasma membrane was not affected by LXR activation (Figure 11A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 11A.

claim: LPS-dependent recruitment of MyD88 and TRAF6 in Flotillin-1-enriched detergent-resistant membrane microdomains was markedly reduced by treatment of iBMDM with GW3965.
source: LPS-dependent recruitment of MyD88 and TRAF6 in Flotillin-1-enriched detergent-resistant membrane microdomains was markedly reduced by treatment of iBMDM with GW3965 (Figure 11B).
evidence: This is supported by membrane fractionation data in Figure 11B.

claim: The ability of LXR agonist to inhibit recruitment of MyD88 and TRAF6 was lost in Abca1-deficient macrophages.
source: Furthermore, the ability of LXR agonist to inhibit recruitment of MyD88 and TRAF6 was lost in Abca1-deficient macrophages.
evidence: This is supported by membrane fractionation data in Figure 11B.

claim: A reduction in raft cholesterol content in response to LXR activation and Abca1 expression leads to alterations in membrane dynamics and/or raft structure and to the disruption of functional TLR4 complexes.
source: These observations suggest that a reduction in raft cholesterol content in response to LXR activation and Abca1 expression leads to alterations in membrane dynamics and/or raft structure and to the disruption of functional TLR4 complexes.
evidence: This is inferred from the membrane fractionation and signaling data.

claim: Downstream MAPK and NF-κB signaling and inflammatory gene expression are repressed as a result of disruption of functional TLR4 complexes.
source: Therefore, downstream MAPK and NF-κB signaling and inflammatory gene expression are repressed.
evidence: This is inferred from the signaling and gene expression data.

claim: An array of inflammatory genes was induced by LPS in spleen and lung of mice.
source: Analysis of gene expression in spleen and lung 2 hr after LPS treatment revealed that an array of inflammatory genes was induced by LPS as expected (Figure 12).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo gene expression data in Figure 12.

claim: LPS-induced inflammatory gene expression was substantially attenuated by LXR agonist treatment in wild-type mice.
source: This induction was substantially attenuated by LXR agonist treatment in wild-type mice, whereas little if any inflammatory repression was observed in mice lacking expression of Abca1 in macrophages (Figure 12).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo gene expression data in Figure 12.

claim: Little if any inflammatory repression was observed in mice lacking expression of Abca1 in macrophages.
source: This induction was substantially attenuated by LXR agonist treatment in wild-type mice, whereas little if any inflammatory repression was observed in mice lacking expression of Abca1 in macrophages (Figure 12).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo gene expression data in Figure 12.

claim: The ability of LXRs to repress inflammation in macrophages derives primarily from their ability to regulate cellular cholesterol metabolism through Abca1.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the ability of LXRs to repress inflammation in macrophages derives primarily from their ability to regulate cellular cholesterol metabolism through Abca1.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the in vivo and in vitro data.

claim: There is an unexpected connection between Abca1-dependent membrane cholesterol distribution and TLR4-mediated inflammatory signaling.
source: They further reveal an unexpected connection between Abca1-dependent membrane cholesterol distribution and TLR4-mediated inflammatory signaling.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental data.

claim: LXRs reciprocally regulate lipid metabolism and inflammation.
source: LXRs reciprocally regulate lipid metabolism and inflammation.
evidence: This is a general statement about LXR function supported by the data.

claim: Both lipid metabolism and inflammation are central to the pathogenesis of metabolic diseases such as atherosclerosis and diabetes.
source: Both of these processes are central to the pathogenesis of metabolic diseases such as atherosclerosis and diabetes (Castrillo et al., 2003a, 2003b; Joseph et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The transrepression model has heretofore been believed to be the sole mechanism underlying LXR's anti-inflammatory effects.
source: This has heretofore been believed to be the sole mechanism underlying LXR's anti-inflammatory effects.
evidence: This is a statement about prior beliefs in the field.

claim: LXR-mediated transcriptional repression of endogenous inflammatory genes is principally dependent on LXR's capacity for transactivation.
source: The present study suggests that LXR-mediated transcriptional repression of endogenous inflammatory genes is principally dependent on LXR's capacity for transactivation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Abca1 induction represses TLR-induced NF-κB and MAPK pathway activation by reducing the cholesterol content of detergent-resistant membrane domains.
source: We find that Abca1 induction represses TLR-induced NF-κB and MAPK pathway activation by reducing the cholesterol content of detergent-resistant membrane domains.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 6, 7, and 9.

claim: Direct transcriptional activation underlies the dual biological functions of LXRs in metabolism and inflammation.
source: These findings reveal a previously unrecognized mechanism for LXR-mediated inflammatory repression in which inflammatory repression is secondary to activation-dependent changes in cellular lipid metabolism.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: LXR agonist did not repress endogenous inflammatory gene expression in the absence of RXRα and RXRβ.
source: Although we cannot exclude the possibility that trans-repression may operate in certain contexts, LXR agonist did not repress endogenous inflammatory gene expression in the absence of RXRα and RXRβ in our system, suggesting that LXR/RXR heterodimers were mediating repression.
evidence: This is supported by the RXR knockdown experiments.

claim: LXR/RXR heterodimers were mediating inflammatory repression.
source: Although we cannot exclude the possibility that trans-repression may operate in certain contexts, LXR agonist did not repress endogenous inflammatory gene expression in the absence of RXRα and RXRβ in our system, suggesting that LXR/RXR heterodimers were mediating repression.
evidence: This is inferred from the RXR knockdown experiments.

claim: The nuclear receptor SF-1 can be modified by SUMO in its hinge region and this modification has been shown to be functionally important for gene repression in vivo.
source: Interestingly, the nuclear receptor SF-1 can be modified by SUMO in its hinge region and this modification has been shown to be functionally important for gene repression in vivo (Campbell et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The repressive effects of SUMOylated SF-1 are mediated by direct binding of SF-1 to response elements in its target promoters.
source: In contrast to the LXR transrepression model, however, the repressive effects of SUMOylated SF-1 are mediated by direct binding of SF-1 to response elements in its target promoters.
evidence: This is a statement about SF-1 mechanism from prior literature.

claim: Prior studies from the authors' group suggested that LXR-mediated inflammatory repression was not mediated by the inhibition of nuclear translocation or DNA binding of NF-κB and AP-1.
source: Prior studies from our group suggested that LXR-mediated inflammatory repression was not mediated by the inhibition of nuclear translocation or DNA binding of NF-κB and AP-1 (Castrillo et al., 2003a, 2003b).
evidence: This refers to prior work by the authors.

claim: The prior studies likely had technical limitations that prevented appreciation of the effects of LXR on NF-κB signaling.
source: In retrospect, these studies likely had technical limitations that prevented us from appreciating the effects of LXR on NF-κB signaling.
evidence: This is a reflection on prior work.

claim: The DNA probe used in prior studies is not predicted to have high affinity for the LPS-induced p65-p50 heterodimer.
source: Our prior studies did not define which NF-κB isoforms were bound to our DNA probe, and according to a recent comprehensive analysis of DNA binding by NF-κB proteins (Siggers et al., 2012), the sequence we used is not predicted to have high affinity for the LPS-induced p65-p50 heterodimer (Hoffmann and Baltimore, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on NF-κB binding.

claim: Subsequent analysis revealed previously unrecognized impairments in NF-κB and MAPK signaling in the setting of LXR activation.
source: Our subsequent analysis of IκB phosphorylation, p65 nuclear translocation, and p65 recruitment to gene promoters has revealed previously unrecognized impairments in NF-κB and MAPK signaling in the setting of LXR activation.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 6-8.

claim: Abca1-deficient macrophages contain more cholesterol and TLR4 protein in plasma membrane lipid rafts and this results in enhanced inflammatory signaling upon LPS treatment.
source: Previous studies have reported that Abca1-deficient macrophages contain more cholesterol and TLR4 protein in plasma membrane lipid rafts and that this results in enhanced inflammatory signaling upon LPS treatment (Koseki et al., 2007; Zhu et al., 2008, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Abca1 expression is important for the ability of LXR to inhibit signaling from TLRs 2, 4 and 9–all of which use MyD88 as a key adaptor.
source: We found that Abca1 expression is important for the ability of LXR to inhibit signaling from TLRs 2, 4 and 9–all of which use MyD88 as a key adaptor.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 10.

claim: LXR activation leads to the induction of an entire cascade of genes involved in cellular lipid homeostasis.
source: LXR activation leads to the induction of an entire cascade of genes involved in cellular lipid homeostasis (Calkin and Tontonoz, 2012; Hong and Tontonoz, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Additional LXR target genes involved in lipid handling may also contribute to effects on inflammation.
source: Although Abca1 is clearly a major contributor, our data do not exclude the involvement of other factors. In our view, it is likely that additional LXR target genes involved in lipid handling may also contribute to effects on inflammation.
evidence: This is speculation about additional mechanisms.

claim: The phospholipid-remodeling enzyme Lpcat3 affects inflammatory signaling in hepatocytes in the setting of obesity.
source: One attractive additional player is the phospholipid-remodeling enzyme Lpcat3, which we have recently shown affects inflammatory signaling in hepatocytes in the setting of obesity (Rong et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.
